title: Recursive sequence
text:
A recursive sequence is a sequence where each term is calculated using the previous few terms of the sequence. The arguably most famous one is the fibonacci numbers.

Number walls[edit]

One tool to spot recursive sequences is a number wall. It can calculate the recursion of any sequence you believe is recursive, as long as it depends linearly on the last few numbers. If it depends on the last n numbers, the first row that will be all zeroes is n rows below your sequence.

Initialization[edit]

To begin a number wall, write a row of ones on the top that continues infinitely. Below it, write your chosen sequence. Then, you can begin using the rules to calculate values.

The cross rule[edit]

To fill in a number wall, use this rule: for any square not on the edges, the value of the square above it times the value of the square below it, plus the value of the square to the left times the value of the square to the right, gives the value of the square squared. Remarkably, if your original sequence is all integers, the entire wall will be.

The big cross rule[edit]

However, it is impossible to work out what number will be two squares below a zero, because zero times anything is still zero. However, there is a second, more complicated rule for this: Two squares below times one square above squared, plus two squares above times one square below squared, is the same as, Two squares left times one square right squared, plus two squares right times one square left squared.

Big windows[edit]

Sometimes, the zeroes will form big squares. Around the edges of those squares, there will be geometric sequences. The ratio of the top going right times the ratio of the bottom going left is the ratio of the left going down times the ratio of the right going up. Then, there is another rule for the terms two squares below the bottom zeroes.
